share.title: Share this proposal
share.copyFailed: Couldn't copy the link — select and copy it from the address bar.
share.message: Europe needs a night train from {origin} to {destination}. {km} km, {stops}, {countries} — here's what it would take:
share.messagePlain: Europe needs a night train from {origin} to {destination}. Here's what it would take:
share.emailBody: This is what a {origin} – {destination} night train would look like — route, timetable and running costs, modelled on the Back-on-Track Target Network:

targetNetwork.fact: Europe ran about 100 night train lines in 2025 — roughly what you are planning here.
targetNetwork.demand: 300 lines by 2035, enough to triple the number of night train passengers.

sevenInTen.fact: 7 in 10 Europeans say they would take a night train instead of a plane, given reasonable conditions.
sevenInTen.demand: dominant booking platforms to be required to show every night train running in their country.

euEmissions.fact: A comprehensive European night train network could avoid 3% of the EU's total greenhouse gas emissions.
euEmissions.demand: the Connecting Europe Facility — nearly €40 billion over six years — to co-finance night train coaches and track access charges.

aviation.fact: Moving travellers from planes to night trains could cut about a quarter of aviation emissions.
aviation.demand: a minimum airline ticket price, to stop fares being dumped below cost.

climate.fact: Taking a night train is about 30 times better for the climate than flying the same route.
climate.demand: VAT scrapped on international rail tickets — international flights are already taxed at 0%.

europeanSleeper.fact: European Sleeper's Brussels–Berlin–Prague route carried more than 230,000 passengers on over 750 trains in its first year.
europeanSleeper.demand: the EU to buy sleeper and couchette coaches and lease them out, so newcomers like this one carry less risk.

flyLess.fact: Nearly half of surveyed night train passengers say they will fly less and take the train more over the next five years.
flyLess.demand: night trains prioritised when train paths are allocated, so the services people want can actually run.

carpatia.fact: Since December 2025 the Carpatia sleeper has linked Przemyśl and Kraków with Vienna, Salzburg and Munich.
carpatia.demand: EU co-funding for pilot routes to Europe's edges — Portugal, Greece, the Nordics, the Baltics.

parisBerlin.fact: A Paris–Brussels–Berlin sleeper has run since March 2026, and Brussels–Milan is due to follow.
parisBerlin.demand: closed border stations reopened — no passenger train has crossed between Irun and Hendaye since 2020.

rollingStock.fact: Europe has roughly 1,500 night train carriages. A full network needs several thousand more by 2035.
rollingStock.demand: the European Investment Bank's Green Rail Investment Platform actually funded — the budget line is still empty.

reuse.fact: About 1,300 publicly funded carriages are being scrapped in France, while Europe is short of sleeper stock.
reuse.demand: EU rules that make reusing second-hand rolling stock possible instead.

network.fact: Back-on-Track is a volunteer network of around 60 active members, with groups in eleven European countries.
network.demand: night trains treated as their own transport segment, exempt from track access surcharges.

expert.pinnedAria: Departure pinned: stays at this time after a recalculation. Click to let it follow the automatic timetable instead.
expert.followsAria: Departure follows the automatic timetable, keeping its distance from it. Click to pin it to this time.
expert.mirroredAria: Opposite direction mirrored around 02:30: departure moved the other way, added minutes reversed. Click to give it its own times.
expert.ownTimesAria: Opposite direction keeps its own times — use the direction switch to edit it. Click to mirror this direction instead.
expert.legAria: Extra minutes on the leg arriving at {stop}
expert.moreAria: One more minute on the leg arriving at {stop}
expert.lessAria: One minute less on the leg arriving at {stop}
expert.droppedAddons: Added minutes were dropped on {legs}: a stop was added in between, so that leg no longer exists.
expert.toggleHint: Shape the timetable yourself: set and pin the first departure, add minutes on single legs, give the return its own times and fix the night. Applies on recalculate.

night.toggleAria: Fixed night: choose the two stops the 00:00–05:00 window is centred between
night.markAria: {stop} — click two stops to place the 00:00–05:00 window between them
night.autoHint: Night: automatic — the whole trip is centred on 02:30. Click the icons of two stops to place it.
night.pendingHint: Now click the other end of the night section.
night.fixedHint: Night between {a} and {b}: the timetable centres 00:00–05:00 on this section and stretches it to five hours if needed.
night.slackHint: {minutes} of these minutes are the night stretch: the section is held to five hours, shared over its legs in proportion to each leg's running time. Minutes you add here count towards the five hours and reduce the stretch.

stopType.boarding: Boarding stop — the train departs before midnight
stopType.alighting: Alighting stop — the train arrives from 05:00

night.legendHint: Night is 00:00–05:00. Boarding stops are left before midnight, alighting stops reached from 05:00; night stops in between sell no tickets.

inputs.title: Choose a scenario and a train composition
inputs.body: Both change every figure below — pick the scenario to evaluate against, and the train composition that would run the route.

impact.title: Key performance indicators
impact.body: Annual demand, modal shift and emissions for this route.

finance.title: Costs and revenue
finance.body: What running the route would cost each year, what tickets would bring in, and the gap between them.
finance.hint: Every cost of a year against every revenue, and the gap: the necessary subsidy, or the surplus once the operator's margin is paid. Click a row for its share and its formula.

viewHints.route: The whole proposal in one figure set: every segment, stop, coach and ticket relation, both directions, a full year. Nothing is allocated — each item is summed.
viewHints.per_trip_pair: One outbound-and-return pair on its own. Differs from the full route only on a Y- or X-shaped route with several pairs.
viewHints.per_trip_pair_per_country: Costs land where the train drives or the event happens, revenue where the passengers sit. Country cells add up to the full route.
viewHints.per_trip_pair_per_section: A physical piece of the trip between two stops, both directions: every cost occurring there and the km-share of everyone on board. Sections overlap, so they do not add up.
viewHints.per_trip_per_stop: One stop call of one direction. Only passengers boarding or alighting here count — the view for whether a call pays. Stop cells add up to the full route.

demand.estimateHint: Placeholder figures derived from route metrics — not yet from a demand model.

impact.placeholder: Demand, modal-shift and CO₂ figures are interim estimates until the demand model lands.

evaluation.viewsLoading: Loading the cost and revenue detail…
evaluation.noClassSplit: No class split in this view.

ownership.copyNote: any change you make is saved as your own copy

priceBasis.hint: All costs and fares are 2032 money, escalated from each source's price year at a documented rate. One exception: rolling stock is bought now, its price stays at 2026.

compare.scenarioBody: Simulate the network, operating conditions and further potential political measures.
compare.scenarioHint: Examine your route under different scenarios. Each combines a rail network with operating conditions and, soon, price measures; the baseline is today's network and rules.
compare.title: Compare across scenarios
compare.body: How the selected train fares under every scenario, and every train under the selected one.
compare.titleHint: Compare the figures across scenarios and compositions: the selected train in every scenario, every train in the selected one, on a figure of your choice. The baseline is marked.
compare.zeroLine: 0 — below the line no subsidy is needed
compare.breakEven: The tick marks break-even — amber needs a subsidy, green pays for itself
compare.measuresNone: Measures: none — today's prices and taxes
compare.hsrInert: This formation is not built for high-speed lines, so the permission changes nothing for it

axes.networkPreviewHint: We're currently preparing to route on the 2032 network. This will also include routing via expected future infrastructure implementations. Stay tuned!
axes.hsr: Night trains may use high-speed lines
axes.optTtNeedsHsr: Optimised timetables are only modelled together with high-speed lines.
axes.measuresHint: We're currently preparing to add further political measures to our scenario analysis. Stay tuned!

measure.tac: Track access at direct costs only

kpiHints.journeyTime: Scheduled time of one direction (the average of both), first departure to last arrival, incl. stops, braking, acceleration and timetable buffer.
kpiHints.pax: Passengers carried per year in both directions: the demand you set, as far as the train's classes can seat it.
kpiHints.paxKm: Each passenger trip times the distance travelled. The basis of the revenue per km and of the CO₂e saving.
kpiHints.subsidy: What the route needs per year to cover all costs and the operator's margin after ticket and other revenue. A surplus shows as none.
kpiHints.shiftAir: Would otherwise have flown; the share grows with journey length (none under 300 km, all from 1,200 km). Interim manual demand model — an automatic one is coming.
kpiHints.shiftOther: The remaining passengers: half would have driven, half would not have travelled at all (induced trips). Interim manual demand model — an automatic one is coming.
kpiHints.co2: Greenhouse gas avoided per year, incl. aviation's non-CO₂ warming: shifted passenger-km at the plane's or car's factor, less the train's. Induced trips count against it.
kpiHints.subsidyPerT: Necessary subsidy divided by the CO₂e saved: what one tonne avoided costs the public. 0 when the route needs no subsidy.

info.departures: Operating days per year times two directions. Follows the frequency and the months the train runs.
info.trainKm: Departures times the route length, both directions, per year.
info.places: Departures times the places in the selected formation, all classes.
info.placeKm: Train-km times the places offered: the capacity the route puts on the rails per year.
info.utilisation: Share of offered place-km actually sold, from the interim demand assumption.

settings.divider: The full cost breakdown, and the details behind it
settings.title: Detail settings
settings.body: Compare and choose the train composition; what the demand figures rest on.
settings.mobileCard: The cost breakdown and the details need a wider screen — evaluated with {composition}, {frequency}.

demand.intro: Passenger numbers are an interim assumption, not a demand model: every train is filled to the same share of its places on every leg, and ticket prices follow a per-km fare by class.
demand.source: Demand source: uniform utilisation of the offered places (interim), to be replaced by a mode-choice model.
demand.prices: Prices: per-km fares by accommodation class, calibrated on current operators.
demand.modes: Competing modes: air and car shares are fixed factors until the demand model lands.
demand.placeholder: Demand settings become editable once the demand model exists.

breakdown.cateringDeduction: Catering costs {value} — taken off the total
breakdown.verdictSurplus: Revenue exceeds cost by {above}: margin {margin} + surplus {surplus}
breakdown.verdictSubsidy: Necessary subsidy {subsidy} — enough for the operator to earn its margin of {margin}

details.title: Details
details.body: What runs the route, what it costs to operate and to use, and who rides it.
details.staleOne: The {what} changed. Panels that depend on it wait for the recalculation.
details.staleMany: The {what} changed. Panels that depend on them wait for the recalculation.

schedule.title: Schedule
schedule.caption: days per week, average over the year
schedule.info: How often the train runs, as one average over the year. Departures, train-km and place-km follow from it; trainsets are the rakes the cycle needs at this frequency.
schedule.operatingDaysNote: {days} operating days a year · which weekdays is not modelled

prices.title: Places and prices
prices.caption: {composition} · {places} places
prices.info: What the train offers and charges, per class: a base fare with a fixed and a distance term, additional services, and a net catering contribution. Fares do not change demand.
prices.weightedAverage: average per passenger, weighted by places

operation.compareInfo: Every composition of the catalogue evaluated on this route under the selected scenario, so the figures compare with each other and with nothing else.
operation.selectedInfo: The composition the figures were computed with, and what one trip costs to run: the rakes and their upkeep, the locomotive hours and the people on board.
operation.onePairOfMany: figures for one trip pair of several

tac.title: Track access charges
tac.info: What each infrastructure manager charges for the run over its network, country by country, on the terms that country levies: distance, weight, places, stops, revenue share.
tac.strip: Track access charges, from one trip

stations.title: Station access charges
stations.info: One charge per stop call, levied by the station's own infrastructure manager at that country's rate. Every stop of the trip is a call, the terminals included.
stations.strip: Station access, from one trip ({cycle} stop events per cycle, {year} per year)

facilities.title: Service facilities — parking
facilities.info: Stabling between arrival and the next departure at each terminal, on the basis that country prices, plus the power drawn while standing. One stay per location and day.
facilities.caption: one stay per terminal per operating day
facilities.perTripRow: Per trip — one stay, averaged over both ends
facilities.none: No stabling priced on this route.

energy.title: Energy
energy.info: Traction energy for the run, country by country: the kWh drawn over its kilometres at its tariff, day and night rate where it has a night band, plus any catenary charge.

year.title: Infrastructure per year
year.info: The four infrastructure lines of the cost breakdown per year, each with its cost per train-kilometre and its share of the total — the same figures as under Costs and revenue.

infrastructure.defaultLegend: marks a figure priced from the EU-average default because the country or stop has no value of its own.

overhead.cateringOutside: Catering ({value} per trip) is outside: it is a net figure, its own overhead already inside it.
overhead.marginNote: Deducted in the net result — not a cost paid to anyone.

variable.title: Variable overhead
variable.covers: Covers sales, distribution and customer service.
variable.info: The operator's selling costs, charged as a share of ticket revenue rather than of the full cost. Catering is outside the base: its contribution is already net of overhead.
variable.caption: a share of ticket revenue

fixed.title: Fixed overhead
fixed.info: The operator's running of itself, charged as a share of its other operating costs — not of variable overhead, and not of the infrastructure charges paid to somebody else.
fixed.caption: a share of the operator's other costs

margin.title: Expected margin
margin.info: The operating profit the operator is expected to keep, as a share of ticket revenue. Nobody receives it: it is subtracted in the net result, so a route can need a subsidy with all bills paid.
margin.caption: a share of ticket revenue
margin.covers: The operating profit the operator is expected to keep. Not a cost paid to anyone.

overhead.fixedBaseItems: Staff, locomotive lease, coach maintenance, on-board service, coach amortisation, financing, cleaning, shunting. Not in it: variable overhead, and everything paid to infrastructure managers.

follows.title: What follows
follows.caption: {composition} · per year, both directions
follows.info: What the schedule and prices earn with the committed demand: passengers, place-km sold, utilisation and revenue per year. Demand edits show only after a recalculation.
follows.noDemand: No calculated demand yet — recalculate to see what the schedule and the prices earn.
follows.vatRate: {rate} ({countries}) · not in the cost and revenue calculation
follows.previewHint: Preview from the schedule and prices against the committed demand. Recalculate to apply them to Train operation, Overhead and the KPI grid.

potential.title: Potential demand
potential.info: Passengers per year over both directions who would take this route. Four levels give a starting figure; any figure can be typed. What a train cannot seat is not served.
potential.perDeparture: {n} per departure at {days} days a week

groupsPanel.title: Demand by traveller group
groupsPanel.caption: shares of the total · classes in order of preference
groupsPanel.info: How the demand splits into traveller groups and which classes each group books, in order. Allocated in rounds by a fixed rule, so a recalculation reproduces the same figures.
groupsPanel.sumOff: Shares sum to {sum} % — the groups then ask for {n}, not the total.
groupsPanel.rule: {rule} % of each group choose by the rule — first listed class until full, then the next; {rest} % pick any other class on their list, evenly.

ladder.title: Utilisation by composition
ladder.info: The same demand on every composition of the family, read as a utilisation per train. The dashed tail is demand no listed class could seat. Click a composition to select it.
ladder.sameDemand: the same demand on every composition ·
ladder.atFrequency: at {days} days per week, {departures} departures a year
ladder.legendCount: number after the bar: the composition’s places
ladder.legendMiss: dashed below: demand not served (figure on the selected composition)

od.title: Demand by OD pair
od.caption: shares of the demand · filled from the stop weights, pin the pairs you know
od.info: The share of the demand each boarding–alighting pair gets, from one weight per stop: a preset or your own, cells pinnable. It moves place-km and revenue, not heads.
od.noRoute: The OD pairs appear once the route has been calculated.
od.hint: Rows board, columns alight; a cell is the pair’s share of the demand, its journey below. Type a share to pin it (●); the margins hold the stop weights that fill the rest — a preset writes them, you can overwrite them. Night stops sell nothing and are not shown.
od.droppedPins: Pins on pairs the route no longer sells were dropped at the last calculation: {pairs}.
od.figuresNote: The stop weights are the request’s few numbers; pinned cells travel with them.

tabHints.demand: How many travel, who they are, where they board and alight — the demand you set, seated on this train.
tabHints.supply: How often the train runs and what each place costs: the schedule and the tariff the revenue is built from.
tabHints.operation: The train itself: every composition on this route, and the rakes, locomotive hours and crew the selected one needs per trip.
tabHints.infrastructure: What infrastructure managers charge, country by country: track access, station calls, stabling and traction energy.
tabHints.overhead: The operator's own shares on top of the direct costs: variable and fixed overhead, and the margin it is expected to keep.

proposal.routeStatsHint: The path comes from a rail routing engine on OpenStreetMap track. Average speed covers the whole journey, stops included, and changes with the selected composition.

gallery.heading: Bring the night trains back on track!

pitch.network: We at Back-on-Track are drawing up a Target Network 2032: around 300 night train connections across the continent, twice as many as today, carrying three times the passengers.
pitch.contribute: This is where you come in. Pick two cities, draw the night train of your dreams on a real map of the European rail network, and see right away what it would cost, how much public money it would need and how much CO₂ it would save — realistic timetables, twelve train compositions, all of it free and open source.
pitch.study: The best suggestions become the backbone of our study for a European night train network in 2032, which we will present to the European Commission and to national transport authorities, and everyone who contributes gets credited. Curious about the numbers behind all this? Have a look at {source}.
